rv.q: The cast, needless to say, couldn't be better.
It is a credit to Metcalf’s gifts that maybe, just maybe, we understand a little bit better why Nora left and Hillary stayed.
Directed firmly and dryly by Joe Mantello, Hillary and Clinton is cogent, snappy and perceptive about political and emotional realities.
She lets you know how much her character both knows and hates.
This is Hillary’s life as it was, is and apparently ever will be, even in an alternative universe.
But all the moments don’t really add up.
Hillary and Clinton reminds us, if anyone dared forget, why she’s so exciting, with her great intelligence and great versatility and her surplus of fierce, nervous energy that barely seems contained.
Ultimately, it feels neither sufficiently contemplative nor revelatory, its ruefulness becoming merely a punishment.
Both give impeccable if somewhat detached performances.
Not even two of the brightest stage stars

The only thing wrong in this fictionalized visit to the 2008 primary — the one that saw Barack Obama claim the Democratic nomination for president over Hillary — is that playwright Hnath, Tony nominated for "A Doll's House, Part 2," has brought nothing of substance to the table.
No matter how you feel about the Clintons you’ll likely find it a once-over-lightly disappointment.

Our humanity belongs in our politics as a reminder of our vulnerability, not as a target for sand in the gears that grind out thoughtful solutions when grounded in what is truly important: protecting the dignity of us all.
That’s an especially spectacular achievement here.
Regardless of where you fall on the political spectrum, the repercussions of that line, 11 years later, will knock the wind out of you.
It’s a slim, impressionistic portrait.
The give-and-take ease of their performances is marvelous.
The play is by turns provocative and poignant, smart and funny.

One might wonder if, a century or so from now, audiences might be able to see Hillary and Clinton with fresh eyes, uninformed by public knowledge and public opinion. But for now, it's those previous opinions we hold that act as additional characters in this vibrant social commentary comedy about the job of getting elected.

The play is as zippy as A Doll’s House, Part 2, but whereas that felt new, fresh, and subversive, Hillary and Clinton feels like very old and well-trodden ground, a mash-up of every single argument you’ve ever heard (with very little new insight) in favor and against Hillary Clinton.
Metcalf, on the stage throughout the entire production, never loses her cool, raises her voice, or fails to keep us wrapped in her easy natural presence.
It has a downbeat and depressing aura and very little occurs.

Don‘t know how much else of this docudrama is true, but of course the real sordid story is how both of these corrupt politicians attempted to manipulate voters (and each other) and how the one who succeeded was no better than the one who lost.

cn.t: Metcalf and Lithgow deliver strong performances in Hnath's speculative 2008 drama, but critics find the play itself smart yet slight, offering witty dialogue without deep insights into the Clintons' marriage or politics.

sg.ra: 805-seat intimate Shubert house; center Orchestra D-F is the consensus best pick across Headout, SeatPlan, and TickPick. Rows A-D play well for plays/intimate-drama given Golden's small footprint. SeatPlan notes mezzanine overhang begins at Row L with 'minimal' effect, so orchestra rear rows remain viable.
Headout and TickPick both flag center G-L as the sweet spot for value — priced below front orchestra but still before the Row L overhang line. In an 805-seat house these rows feel close regardless.

Front Mezz rows A-C center are the #2 premium pick after center orchestra — elevation gives a clean overhead line on the small Golden stage. SeatPlan flags a safety bar that can distract Row A slightly, and legroom is noted as 'slightly cramped for taller patrons.'

SeatPlan calls rear mezz 'surprisingly good' because the 805-seat footprint keeps even back rows close. Rake is described as well-designed with good elevation over Front Mezz. Legroom is the main knock — 'cramped' with narrow pitch.
